sections.title: Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT)
sections.content: The GHT compares 5 zones in the superior hemifield to corresponding zones in the inferior hemifield. It is the most sensitive HFA test for early glaucomatous damage. Results: 'Outside Normal Limits' (highly specific for glaucoma), 'Borderline' (warrants follow-up), or 'Within Normal Limits'. 'General Reduction in Sensitivity' may occur if the entire field is depressed.

rows: Global index representing remaining visual function; 100% = normal, 0% = perimetrically blind.
Measures localized field loss (irregularity); high PSD indicates localized scotoma/glaucoma.
Average departure from age-matched norms; reflects overall field depression (cataract vs. glaucoma).

sections.title: Pattern Analysis: Temporal Wedge vs. Nasal Step

branches: Temporal Wedge: Often indicates early nerve fiber bundle defects or chiasmal lesions
Nasal Step: Classic early glaucoma indicator; asymmetrical loss across the horizontal meridian
Paracentral Scotoma: Often the earliest manifestation of glaucomatous optic neuropathy

sections.title: Red Flags in Perimetry
content: False Negative Rate > 20% (Inattention or advanced disease)

content.explanation: Reliability (Fixation/False Positives), Indices (MD/PSD), GHT, Interpretation (Pattern of loss), Diagnosis correlation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Check Reliability Indices (Fixation losses, false +/-).
Step 2: Inspect Global Indices (MD and PSD).
Step 3: Analyze Pattern Deviation plots (not just Total Deviation) to remove cataract bias.
Step 5: Correlate field defect location with Disc/RNFL (e.g., inferotemporal rim thinning correlates with superior field loss).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pattern Deviation is the 'Gold Standard' for identifying glaucomatous localized loss, as it filters out generalized depression.
A 'Nasal Step' is often the first reproducible sign of early glaucoma, occurring due to the anatomical distribution of retinal nerve fibers.
Always repeat the first visual field test; the 'Learning Effect' often artificially inflates severity on the first attempt.
Temporal wedge defects can mimic glaucoma but should trigger a search for chiasmal pathology (e.g., pituitary adenoma) via MRI.
